questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Over an Unbounded Interval
questions.problem:
Compute $P(X>8)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}},\, & x\ge 3, \\ 0,\, & x<3.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>8) & =P(8<X<\infty ) \\  & ={\int }_{8}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{8}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{3}{x}]}_{8}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Given a PDF
questions.problem:
Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}k{e}^{6x},\, & x\le 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=k{e}^{6x}$ on the interval $-\infty <x\le 0,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}k{e}^{6x}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}k{e}^{6x}\,\text{d}x={[\frac{k}{6}{e}^{6x}]}_{-\infty }^{0}=\frac{k}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\frac{k}{6}=1\,⟹\,k=6.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Over an Unbounded Interval
questions.problem:
Compute $P(X>4)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<1, \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},\, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>4) & =P(4<X<\infty ) \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}]}_{4}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Given a PDF
questions.problem:
Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{(2x-1)^{2}},\, & x\ge 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=\frac{k}{(2x-1)^{2}}$ on the interval $x\ge 2,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{k}{(2x-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{k}{(2x-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{k}{2(2x-1)}\,{|}_{2}^{\infty }=\frac{k}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\frac{k}{6}=1\,⟹\,k=6.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Given a PDF
questions.problem:
Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}k{e}^{3x+2},\, & x\le 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=k{e}^{3x+2}$ on the interval $x\le 0,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}k{e}^{3x+2}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}k{e}^{3x+2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{k}{3}{e}^{3x+2}\,{|}_{-\infty }^{0}=\frac{k{e}^{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\frac{k{e}^{2}}{3}=1\,⟹\,k=\frac{3}{{e}^{2}}.
$$
